content:
A claim about how a former Apple employee could have accessed confidential files after leaving to join OpenAI has been knocked down by court filings.

There was speculation that the file access may have simply been an accident, because iCloud arrangements for Apple employees appeared to be somewhat chaotic — but Apple says this isn't the case…

Quick recap

Apple last month filed suit against OpenAI, accusing it of stealing trade secrets related to a hardware project. One of the claims focused on a former Apple employee named Chang Liu, who subsequently joined OpenAI. Here's roughly the timeline:

  • July 10: Apple sues OpenAI, accusing a former Apple employee of systematically stealing Apple trade secrets to benefit the OpenAI hardware team they subsequently joined
  • July 10: OpenAI issues a brief denial
  • July 14: OpenAI updates its response to say it has seen no evidence to support Apple's claims
  • August 3: OpenAI publishes a blog post attacking Apple's lawsuit
  • August 4: Apple applies for a temporary restraining order to prevent "irreparable harm"

The iCloud mess

OpenAI says that an information security flaw inside Apple resulted in the former employee retaining "unnecessary" access to confidential files after leaving.

Earlier this week, The Information published a report suggesting this was the iCloud arrangement mess OpenAI was referring to.

The report noted that, while Apple would remove former employees' access to corporate-managed iCloud folders, it appears many files had likely been shared to the employee's personal account — which they not only retained access to after leaving, but could even receive push updates on.

In other words, former employees' personal devices could automatically receive updates on confidential files without any wrongdoing on their part.

Apple says this isn't true

However, John Gruber at Daring Fireball notes that Apple explicitly states in its court filings that the files were not stored in iCloud.

Gruber says the files were almost certainly stored on Box, the cloud storage service that has been widely deployed inside Apple.

9to5Mac's take

At this point it's still a case of competing claims, and we'll need to wait for the case to be properly heard to sort out what's true and what isn't.

But there does seem to be a tacit admission from Apple that there's an iCloud mess. The reasoning behind this setup is reportedly to avoid Apple employees needing to carry both a work and personal iPhone. While that's understandable, it does seem to have created a significant security hole.
